analysis.investment_thesis: HRS Aluglaze fails both legs of the Magic Formula decisively — a P/E of 105 implies an earnings yield near 0.95% (vs. my 12%+ threshold), and an ROE of 0.34% signals return on capital nowhere near the 20%+ I require. This is the textbook opposite of "cheap and good" — it is expensive and unprofitable.
key_strengths: Exposure to India's construction/façade demand cycle
Small INR 540 Cr cap leaves room for operational scale-up if margins normalize
key_risks: Earnings yield ~0.95% — one of the most overvalued setups possible
ROE 0.34% suggests capital is essentially earning nothing
Commoditized fabrication/installation business with thin, cyclical margins
red_flags: P/E of 105 on negligible profitability — speculative pricing
ROE <1% implies EBIT/capital is likely in low single digits
Recently listed micro-cap with no demonstrated track record of high ROIC
analysis.detailed_analysis:
The Magic Formula ranks companies on earnings yield (EBIT/EV) and return on capital. Even generously assuming EBIT roughly tracks net income, a trailing P/E of 105 implies an earnings yield under 1% — I want 12%+ and ideally 15%+. On the quality side, ROE of 0.34% tells me capital deployed into this aluminium fabrication business is not earning anywhere near a cost-of-capital return, let alone the 20–25% ROIC I look for. Failing both screens is disqualifying; there is no mechanical reason to own this.

Qualitatively, aluminium windows, doors and curtain-wall installation is a competitive, working-capital-heavy, project-execution business with limited pricing power and lumpy revenue recognition — exactly the kind of industry where durable high ROIC is rare. The 72.49% promoter holding is a positive governance signal, but it does not change the arithmetic. At this valuation, the market is pricing in a dramatic margin expansion that the current financials do not support. Pass until either price collapses materially or ROIC structurally steps up above 20%.
